industrial ag mega-zine update:

i started researching USSR agriculture for the next part of the zine, and swiftly started shriveling into a husk, so i'm changing course: i am making a spread about potatoes.

standardized high-yield potato vareties were already quite well-developed and established before WWII, so the post-war story is less about breeding and more about utilization, which means "research on how to get more uses out of the crop".

it turns out that researchers (public and private - USDA was doing loads of research on developing new products for market) had great success turning potatoes into a million things.

and according to industry journals from the time, they were very happy with how much success they were having with getting people to buy all kinds of potato products. plus, things like dehydrated, frozen, and granulated potato products received a lot of uptake in institutions - the military, schools, hospitals, fast-food restaurants. a mass-produced crop for a mass-managed and mass-fed population.

so why was all this utilization research necessary? because farmers were producing loads of potatoes and people weren't buying enough of them in raw form. so it's not like they were trying to feed more people, they were trying to get more people to buy a crop that was producing "too much" year after year. so "how do we get the consumer to buy more?" "how do we get people to eat more potatoes?". that's what it was about.

and having gone through all the research on the green revolution, it's such a stark contrast: in developing countries, america was pushing certain crops and high-intensity agriculture to "feed hungry people", but in the US it was all about making $ and how to push more product. 

i don't know, those two positions aren't inherently at opposite poles, but it does create a strange juxtaposition in my mind.

as a person whose ancestry is based in a potato and wheat part of the world (eastern europe), and who grew up eating loads and loads of delicious potato, potatoes are near and dear to my heart (even though i rarely eat them now. they're actually quite expensive here and i often have more access to local starches, like breadfruit, taro, and cooking banana. also, i eat more rice these days. potatoes really are expensive here!)

anyway, here's a picture i found in the course of my research: "engineers in Eastern Regional Research Center pilot plant process mashed potatoes into a continuous sheet that can be broken up into instant potato flakes." what a world! and how nice for industry to have the government running massive labs and even test plants to develop and test new products and processes for you!
